title: Job 40:1–5
context: This unit holds the close of the LORD’s first speech and Job’s first reply together. In 40:1–2 the LORD speaks, asking whether one who argues will contend with the Almighty, and calling the one who argues with God to answer. In 40:3–5 Job speaks: he says he is of small account, asks what he could answer, lays his hand on his mouth, and says he has spoken once, even twice, and will go no further. Laying a hand on the mouth is a gesture of silence elsewhere in Job (compare Job 21:5; 29:9). Job’s reply is sober and brief; it is commonly read as silence and withdrawal from his case, pointing ahead to his second reply in 42:1–6, whose wording at 42:6 is itself read in more than one way. The LORD does not accept this as the end and speaks again. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about humility before God, while letting the book’s fuller resolution come later.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD continuing to answer Job before Job replies in verses 3–5. The LORD keeps the conversation open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD pressing his question to Job, who will answer briefly in verses 3–5. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a transition within the dialogue.

verses.text: “Shall he who argues contend with the Almighty? He who argues with God, let him answer it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether the one who argues will contend with the Almighty and calling him to answer. Job, who wanted a hearing, now has one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD answering Job’s demand for a hearing (compare Job 31:35). Readers in both traditions commonly read the challenge as the setting for Job’s reply that follows.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job answering the LORD after the first speech. His response is brief compared with his earlier speeches.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job’s turn to speak before the LORD resumes. Both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing a short, sober reply from Job to the LORD.

verses.text: “Behold, I am of small account. What will I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying he is of small account and laying his hand on his mouth before the LORD. He falls silent rather than argue further.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see humility in Job’s answer to the LORD, though 42:1–6 still lies ahead. Readers in both traditions commonly avoid overreading this first reply as Job’s last word, and they hold the sense of 42:6 open rather than treating it as a single slogan.

verses.text: I have spoken once, and I will not answer; Yes, twice, but I will proceed no further.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying he has spoken once and twice but will go no further. He withdraws from pressing his case before the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job ceasing his argument while the LORD prepares to speak again. Both traditions commonly read Job’s silence as a real but partial step, with the fuller resolution still to come.
